validated_results.title: Alcohol consumption and the risk of bladder cancer in the Framingham Heart Study.
validated_results.journal: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
validated_results.reason: Original prospective analysis in the Framingham Heart Study reporting incident bladder cancer risk according to alcohol consumption categories.

extraction.comparison_type: Categories of alcohol consumption (highest vs lowest intake categories), with risk-set matched controls

sample_size.excerpt: We used data from 10,125 participants in the Framingham Heart Study to assess the association between total and beverage-specific alcohol consumption and the risk of bladder cancer. For each case of bladder cancer, up to five control subjects were selected and matched on major confounders using a risk set method.

cases.excerpt: During a mean follow-up of 27.3 +/- 10.1 years, there were 126 incident cases of bladder cancer.

comparison.excerpt: We used conditional logistic regression to assess the risk of bladder cancer according to categories of alcohol consumption.

design.excerpt: For each case of bladder cancer, up to five control subjects were selected and matched on major confounders using a risk set method.

timing.excerpt: During a mean follow-up of 27.3 +/- 10.1 years

validated_results.title: Prospective study of alcohol drinking and renal cell cancer risk in a cohort of finnish male smokers.
validated_results.journal: Cancer epidemiology, biomarkers & prevention : a publication of the American Association for Cancer Research, cosponsored by the American Society of Preventive Oncology
validated_results.reason: Prospective cohort of Finnish male smokers reporting multivariate relative risks of incident renal cell cancer by quartiles of total alcohol intake.

extraction.comparison_type: Highest vs lowest quartile of total alcohol intake
extraction.population: Male smokers in the Alpha-Tocopherol, Beta-Carotene (ATBC) Cancer Prevention Study

cases.excerpt: We ascertained 195 incident cases of RCC.

effect_size.excerpt: In multivariate analysis, the relative risks and 95% confidence intervals (CI) of RCC according to increasing quartiles of total alcohol intake were 1.0, 0.91 (0.62-1.33), 0.94 (0.64-1.38), and 0.53 (0.34-0.83), respectively (P value for trend = 0.005); for spirit consumption, 1.0, 0.93 (0.63-1.Fspiait39), 0.84 (0.58-1.20), and 0.55 (0.36-0.85) (P for trend = 0.02); and for beer intake, 1.0, 1.22 (0.85-1.76), 0.83 (0.57-1.22), and 0.55 (0.36-0.85) (P for trend = 0.003). Too few people in this cohort drank wine to assess its association with risk of RCC.

confidence_interval.excerpt: In multivariate analysis, the relative risks and 95% confidence intervals (CI) of RCC according to increasing quartiles of total alcohol intake were 1.0, 0.91 (0.62-1.33), 0.94 (0.64-1.38), and 0.53 (0.34-0.83), respectively (P value for trend = 0.005); for spirit consumption, 1.0, 0.93 (0.63-1.Fspiait39), 0.84 (0.58-1.20), and 0.55 (0.36-0.85) (P for trend = 0.02); and for beer intake, 1.0, 1.22 (0.85-1.76), 0.83 (0.57-1.22), and 0.55 (0.36-0.85) (P for trend = 0.003).

comparison.excerpt: according to increasing quartiles of total alcohol intake

design.excerpt: We prospectively examined the association between total alcohol intake as well as specific types of alcoholic beverage and RCC in a large cohort of Finnish male smokers.

timing.excerpt: Men from the Alpha-Tocopherol, BetaCarotene (ATBC) Cancer Prevention Study were followed for 12 years

continent.excerpt: a large cohort of Finnish male smokers

exposure_measurement.excerpt: Alcohol consumption was assessed at baseline using a questionnaire previously shown to be both reproducible and valid.

validated_results.title: Alcohol consumption and risk of renal cell carcinoma: a prospective study of Swedish women.
validated_results.reason: Population-based prospective cohort of Swedish women reporting rate ratios for incident renal cell carcinoma by alcohol consumption.

extraction.population: Women aged 40-76 years in the Swedish Mammography Cohort

sample_size.excerpt: Thus, we examined the association between alcohol intake and the incidence of RCC by analyzing data from the Swedish Mammography Cohort, a population-based prospective cohort of 59,237 women, aged 40-76 years, who, at baseline in 1987-1990, were cancer free and had completed a food-frequency questionnaire including questions about alcohol consumption. Through June 30, 2004, 132 incident cases of RCC were diagnosed.

cases.excerpt: Through June 30, 2004, 132 incident cases of RCC were diagnosed.

effect_size.excerpt: Women who consumed >4.3 grams per day of alcohol (ethanol) had nonsignificantly lower risk of RCC than did women who consumed <2.5 g/d (RR = 0.71, 95% CI 0.42-1.19); among women > or = 55 years of age at entry into the cohort, corresponding risk estimates were RR = 0.33, 95% CI 0.10-1.05, p for trend = 0.04 and among women with BMI >25 kg/m2, RR = 0.30, 95% CI 0.09-0.97, p for trend = 0.04.

confidence_interval.excerpt: Women who consumed >4.3 grams per day of alcohol (ethanol) had nonsignificantly lower risk of RCC than did women who consumed <2.5 g/d (RR = 0.71, 95% CI 0.42-1.19); among women > or = 55 years of age at entry into the cohort, corresponding risk estimates were RR = 0.33, 95% CI 0.10-1.05, p for trend = 0.04 and among women with BMI >25 kg/m2, RR = 0.30, 95% CI 0.09-0.97, p for trend = 0.04.
